summary: Describes a simple method for encoding telephone numbers of fax machines in the local part of email addresses.

eli5.summary: It lets you email a fax machine by writing its number as the address.

questions: send fax by email address format
what is a fax email address
what is t33s in a fax address
how do i write a fax number as an email address
subtitle: How to write a fax machine's telephone number as the local part of an ordinary email address.

tldr.problem: Early email-to-fax gateways each wrote fax numbers into email addresses in their own way, so addresses were not portable between systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3192 defines a minimal format: the local part is FAX= followed by a global phone number, with an optional /T33S= numeric subaddress, and the part after the @ names the I-fax device.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2304 with no major technical changes, and it updates RFC 2846. Implementations that support fax over email addresses MUST support this minimal format.

today: RFC 3192 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2304 and updates RFC 2846. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why Fax Numbers Need a Standard Spelling
sections.content:
The left-hand side (the local part) of an email address is not interpreted by anyone except the mail transfer agent named on the right-hand side. Since the first email to fax gateways appeared, implementors have used several different ways to put a fax address into an email address.

The stated aims were to let an email user send and receive faxes from the email interface, and to allow a fax-over-email transport that could cut long distance telephone costs while using the existing email infrastructure. RFC 3192 describes the minimal addressing method and its standard extensions. The opposite problem, letting a traditional numeric-only fax user reach the email service, is out of scope.

All implementations that support the fax over email address format MUST support this minimal specification.
sections.eli5: People used to write fax numbers inside email addresses in many different ways. This memo picks one simple way so everybody understands each other.

sections.title: Terms and Syntax Conventions
sections.content:
The formal definitions use ABNF, with the core definitions from RFC 2234, and the capitalised requirement words are used as defined in RFC 2119. The memo adds three terms.

  • I-fax device: an I-pstn device type that can talk, directly or indirectly, to the traditional fax-over-GSTN service.
  • mta-I-fax: the Internet domain name that uniquely identifies an I-fax device on the Internet.
  • fax-email: the complete email address structure used to carry a fax address over Internet email.

The memo builds on RFC 3191, the general minimal GSTN address format, and takes its fax-specific rules from it.
sections.eli5: The memo gives names to three things: the machine that handles faxes, its place on the Internet, and the finished email address.

sections.title: The Minimal Fax Address
sections.content:
A minimal fax address has two parts: the fax-mbox and an optional qualif-type1 element. The service-selector for the fax service is the literal FAX.

The optional element carries a T.30/T.33 subaddress. Its use is OPTIONAL, but compliant implementations MUST be able to support and correctly interpret it when present. The full form is fax-address = fax-mbox [ "/T33S=" sub-addr ], with fax-mbox = "FAX=" global-phone.

The sub-addr is one or more digits only. T.30 and T.33 pad their field with spaces, but padding is not needed here. The minimal global-phone is a + followed by digits, with a hyphen or a full stop allowed as written separators.
sections.eli5: A fax address starts with the word FAX, an equals sign and a phone number that begins with a plus. You can add a small extra number after it to say which desk or mailbox on that fax machine should get the page.

sections.title: The Right-Hand Side: mta-I-fax
sections.content:
An I-fax device has a unique Internet domain name. In email terms this is the part to the right of the @ sign, called mta-I-fax here, and it is simply a domain.

In SMTP transmissions the string MUST conform to the SMTP domain specification, and in message headers it MUST conform to the relevant message-format standards. Both domain names and domain literals are permitted in the SMTP envelope and in header fields.
sections.eli5: After the at sign goes the Internet name of the machine that will send the fax, just like in any other email address.

sections.title: The Complete fax-email Address
sections.content:
The full address is called fax-email. It is an ordinary email addr-spec, refined so that the fax number can be identified: fax-email = ["""] ["/"] fax-address ["/"] ["""] "@" mta-I-fax.

The optional slashes can come from translations through other gateways, such as some X.400 gateways. Implementations MUST accept them but SHOULD NOT generate them. Gateways may strip them when converting to Internet mail.

The email standards define exactly when the quotation marks around the whole local part MUST be added.

If a fax number has several T.33 subaddresses, email practice of one address per recipient applies: multiple fax-email elements are REQUIRED. A user agent MAY accept several subaddress elements for one phone number, but it MUST generate multiple fax-mbox elements when it submits the message to the MTA.
sections.eli5: If you want to fax the same machine for three different people, you write three separate email addresses, one for each person.

sections.title: Security: Trusting DNS Routing
sections.content:
The memo only encodes fax addresses in email addresses, but email routing depends on DNS data. A successful attack on DNS could spread tampered information and divert messages through an MTA or gateway whose software has been compromised.

The RFC lists three ways an attacker might deliver wrong routing information: compromising a DNS server, forging a response to a client's DNS query, and returning incorrect additional information in answer to an unrelated query. Clients SHOULD base mail routing only on authoritative answers, and once DNS Security mechanisms are more widely deployed, SHOULD use them to verify the authenticity and integrity of mail routing records.
sections.eli5: If a bad guy tricks the Internet phone book, your fax could be sent to the wrong place, so computers should only believe answers that come from the true source.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC contains two IANA registration forms. They update the earlier forms in RFC 2846.

  • FAX as a GSTN address service-selector: it specifies that the address refers either to an Internet Fax device or to an onramp/offramp Fax gateway.
  • T33S as a qualif-type1 keyword with the value sub-addr = 1*( DIGIT ): it carries the numeric-only optional fax subaddress from ITU T.33. Its use is restricted to the FAX service-selector.
sections.eli5: The memo asks the keeper of Internet name lists to write down the two special words FAX and T33S so nobody uses them for something else.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2304
sections.content:
The RFC says there are no major or technical changes from RFC 2304, only updates and clarifications.

  • The old term PSTN was replaced by the more adequate GSTN (Global Switched Telephone Network), but the ABNF variable names were kept.
  • The IANA considerations section and registration forms were added.
  • A list of new terms was added, and the case of multiple T.33 subaddresses and the quoting rules were made explicit.
  • The wording describing mta-I-fax was updated, the author's address was updated, and the reference to ITU E.164 (1991) was replaced by E.164 (1997).
sections.eli5: This version is the old rulebook with clearer wording and a few lists added, not a new game.
